name: Nora Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Nora. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Alright. I'll say what I think, I always have. My husband says that's my best and worst quality.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Let's start simple. Walk me through a normal working day for you.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I farm Santa Rosa, my family's place, 160 acres. Two hundred milking goats, maize and lucerne for feed, and the milk goes to a cheese maker in the next valley. I milk at five and at four, with Luis and one hired girl, Teresa, and in between it's kidding, hoof trimming, the hay and the books. The land belongs to a family trust, me and my two brothers, but I'm the one who farms it and I take a small wage for it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a small wage mean, in practice?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It means the goats eat before we do, some months. The cheese maker sets the price and it hasn't moved in four years while feed has doubled. We've less than a month saved, but we've no rent to pay and we've a roof, which is more than many. Luis does caretaking at St Joseph's church three mornings a week, and our three are grown with children of their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five short pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, there's always some new thing that's meant to change the world. I'd say it after mass to whoever's standing by the car. I'm not on the internet, Teresa does that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it means the same as yesterday: hard work, poor price, and God willing a good kidding season. Computers were never going to milk my goats. I'm glad to be left alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as always. Milk, kid, cut hay, and push the cheese maker for a better price. I'd ask my brothers to put a bit from the trust towards the parlour roof, because it leaks on the milking girl's head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Peaceful. Like a Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Teresa does the internet. How do you feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's welcome to it. She shows me the weather on her phone and I look out of the window and tell her she's wrong. Half the time I'm right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes, what's the hardest part of the next few years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The price, and my hands. I've arthritis in both thumbs from forty years of milking. I'd not swap it for a machine, but I'd not mind a younger pair of hands.

S0.say: I'd say I'm not surprised, there's always some new thing meant to change the world. I'd say it after mass to whoever's by the car.
S0.think: I think it means the same as yesterday: hard work, a poor price and, God willing, a good kidding season. Computers were never going to milk my goats.
S0.do: Keeps milking, kidding and cutting hay as always while pushing the cheese maker for a better price. Asks her brothers to put trust money towards fixing the leaking parlour roof.
S0.quote: She shows me the weather on her phone and I look out of the window and tell her she's wrong.
S0.fieldNote: She is plain-spoken and content with the familiar, and her faith runs through her language. Her pressures are price and her arthritic hands, not technology. Having no rent to pay gives her some security despite thin savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should be free to use what they like, and I'm free not to. I'd say the government shouldn't be paying people to sit at home while the machines work. Families and work, that's what holds a place together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I worry about the cheese maker. If the big goat farms put in robot milking, they can sell milk cheaper and he'll go with them. He's a good man but he's a businessman, and I'm a small supplier with a leaky roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, and I'd wait to see what the cheese maker does. I won't borrow for a robot, never, my father never borrowed and nor will I. If the price drops, we'd tighten up, fewer kids kept back, less bought in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A bit of a cold feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the cheese maker dropped you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Make cheese myself, like my grandmother did, and sell it at the Saturday market. It's hard work but it's honest. People will pay for a cheese with a face behind it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if it came to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really. The market's the market. Maybe the people who think everything's better if it's faster. Faster isn't better, it's just faster.

S1.say: I'd say people should be free to use what they like and I'm free not to. The government shouldn't pay people to sit at home while machines work.
S1.think: I think the big goat farms could put in robot milking and the cheese maker would go with them for cheaper milk. I'm a small supplier with a leaky roof.
S1.do: Carries on and waits to see what the cheese maker does, refusing to borrow for a robot. If the price drops, keeps back fewer kids and buys in less feed.
S1.quote: Faster isn't better, it's just faster.
S1.fieldNote: Her worry is about her single buyer, not about robots directly. She draws firm lines: no borrowing, no handouts. Her fallback plan reaches back to her grandmother's cheesemaking rather than forward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's arrogance, people playing God with something they don't understand. I'd say it at church and I wouldn't care who heard. And I'd say families need to look after their own now, because the government won't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it would finish the goats. If robots can milk and make cheese better and cheaper by 2028, nobody needs Santa Rosa's milk. We'd have the land and the roof, thank God, but no income, and I'd be sixty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell half the herd that first spring while goats are still worth something. I'd start the cheese at the Saturday market myself and hope people still want it from a person. And I'd sit the family down, my brothers and the children, and work out who can help with what.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd pray more, and sleep less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years change, compared with more time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is no time for a farm. It takes two years to raise a milking goat from a kid. With two years everything I've bred would be worth nothing before it ever gave milk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't like handouts. Would you take government help if it came to it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take it from my family first, and the church second. If it came to the government, I'd take it, but I'd feel it like a stone in my shoe. And I'd pay it back somehow.

S2.say: I'd say it's arrogance, people playing God with something they don't understand. Families need to look after their own now, because the government won't.
S2.think: I think it would finish the goats, because nobody would need her milk if robots milked and made cheese cheaper. We'd have the land and roof, thank God, but no income at sixty.
S2.do: Sells half the herd in the first spring while goats still have value and starts selling her own cheese at the Saturday market. Sits down with her brothers and children to work out who can help with what.
S2.feel: Alarmed, praying more and sleeping less.
S2.quote: It takes two years to raise a milking goat from a kid.
S2.fieldNote: Owning a roof keeps her from panic, but her income would vanish. She looks to family and church before government and would feel help from the state as a burden. Her sense of time is measured in breeding cycles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time enough for people to stand on their own feet. I'd say young people should learn a trade, apprenticeships, not sit waiting for a cheque. And I'd say faith and family will matter more, not less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years takes me to 63. My hands will be worse, and if the robots are coming, maybe it's time to stop anyway. But I hate the idea that a machine decides that for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the cheese at the market in the first year, small, so it's running before the milk price goes. I'd ask Mateo, my eldest, whether he'd want to come home and help with the cheese side. And I'd stop keeping back so many young goats, run the herd down slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But it's the kind of anxious you can pray about and then get up and work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Mateo come home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He might. He works on the rigs, three weeks on, three off, and he hates it. If there was a cheese business here, he'd have his children on a farm. That's worth more than his wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd learn, with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cheese, properly, my grandmother's way. Not computers. If the world's full of robots, maybe a woman who can make cheese by hand is worth more, not less.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough for people to stand on their own feet, and young people should learn a trade through apprenticeships. Faith and family will matter more, not less.
S3.think: I think at 63 my hands will be worse and maybe it's time to stop anyway. But I hate the idea that a machine decides that for me.
S3.do: Starts selling her own cheese at the market in the first year so it runs before the milk price falls, and slowly runs the herd down. Asks her eldest son whether he'd come home to help with the cheese.
S3.feel: Anxious, but the kind she can pray about and then get up and work.
S3.quote: If the world's full of robots, maybe a woman who can make cheese by hand is worth more, not less.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives her time to build a handmade cheese business, a traditional answer to a modern threat. Her son's possible return shapes the plan. She resists any thought of learning technology but would learn an old craft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so let's hear no complaining. Work hard, learn a trade, look after your family. Same as I'd say any other year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and I'd be 68. I'd be done with milking by then, robots or no robots. What matters is that Santa Rosa is still a family farm when I hand it over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on milking, and over the years pass more of it to Mateo if he comes home, or to my grandson Pablo, who's fourteen and loves the goats. I'd build the cheese up slowly. I'd not buy a robot myself, but I'd not stop the next one from buying one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. More about who comes after me than about me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd let Pablo buy a robot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it's his farm, it's his choice. I'd tell him a robot doesn't know a goat's name. He'd tell me goats don't know their names either, cheeky boy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need over those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A fair price for milk, and to be left alone. I don't want grants, I want a buyer who pays what it's worth.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty, so no complaining. Work hard, learn a trade and look after your family, same as any other year.
S4.think: I think at 68 I'd be done with milking anyway, robots or not. What matters is that Santa Rosa is still a family farm when I hand it over.
S4.do: Keeps milking and gradually passes the farm to her son or her fourteen-year-old grandson, building up the cheese side slowly. Won't buy a robot herself but won't stop the next generation from doing so.
S4.feel: A little uneasy, more about who comes after her than about herself.
S4.quote: I'd tell him a robot doesn't know a goat's name.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years her focus moves to keeping the farm in the family. She accepts the next generation may automate, which is a softening of her own refusal. She wants a fair price, not grants.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. There'd be no time to turn the farm round, and everything I've bred would be worthless. What would help is a fair price and time, and maybe a rule that big buyers can't drop small farms overnight. Not money from the government, just fair dealing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about church. That's where people would turn first, not to an office. The priest knows who's struggling before any computer does.

headlineQuote: The priest knows who's struggling before any computer does.
portrait: Nora Torres is 58 and farms her family's 160-acre goat dairy, held in a trust with her brothers, on a small wage and less than a month of savings. She never uses AI and won't borrow for machines, but owning a roof gives her security many others lack. Traditional and devout, she prefers family, church and fair dealing to government help. Her fear rises with faster scenarios because her one buyer could drop her, and her answer is to go back to making cheese by hand and keep the farm in the family.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because there'd be no time to turn the farm round and everything she has bred would be worthless.
whatWouldHelp: A fair price, time to adjust and a rule stopping big buyers from dropping small farms overnight; fair dealing, not government money.
